name: Zane Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zane Fischer, 43. I left school early and joined construction late, so I'm still the junior person on a crew doing framing and general jobs. I unload sheet goods, set studs and fetch the fixings; the lead checks my cuts because I can still drift off the line. I like the moment a bare room takes shape. I don't like pretending I understand a drawing when I need to ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household have to work with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Dev works on and off at a school office, and our two children are seven and twelve. We pay a mortgage and have about four months of expenses saved; my wage is typical for the site, but the office hours vary. There are some other builders nearby, not a huge pool. I've tried AI now and then for reading a tricky material note, but I ask a coworker before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew it's fine if the office saves half an hour on forms, as long as they still send the right studs. I'd say our wages come from getting the frame right, not from a faster email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep working, but Dev's school-office hours can change and one quiet month on site would use our reserve. The AI plateau does not remove that worry; I'm junior enough that a small mistake can cost me the next call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the framing shifts and ask the lead to check my layout before cutting. In the first year I'd try the AI material-note reader only on a job where the lead can compare it with the drawing; if it gets a size wrong, I'll stop using it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The technology is small in this version, but our two wages are not as steady as the mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which note trips you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A window schedule sometimes gives the rough opening size in a different column from the finished size. Last month I nearly cut to the wrong figure until the lead pointed at the header.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel embarrassed asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd rather ask once than make the apprentice after me carry a replacement bundle upstairs.

say: I would accept **form savings** if material deliveries remain accurate.
I would say our wages still depend on a **sound frame**.
think: My **site wage** probably continues, though quiet months can use our reserve.
Dev’s **school-office hours** also vary, making the mortgage less comfortable.
do: Keep taking **framing shifts** and have layouts checked before cutting.
Try an **AI note reader** only where the lead can verify sizes.
feel: **Uneasy** about household hours despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: The technology is small in this version, but our two wages are not as steady as the mortgage bill.
fieldNote: Zane places the plateau beside **variable household hours**, rather than treating little AI change as full security.
His **occasional AI use** stays narrow and checked against a lead’s drawing after a near mistake on window sizes.

steps.text: Keep taking paid framing shifts and ask lead to check layouts
Try AI material-note reader on one lead-checked drawing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask at the site meeting who checks a software plan before the crew is blamed for missing it. If the office gets smaller, they should give us proper time to learn the new paperwork rather than slipping it into lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The saw and hammer still need people for now, but software could let a contractor promise more work with fewer hands. I could lose site days before any robot arrives, and our four months of savings would go quickly if Dev's hours dipped too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a union organiser to bring the crews together on how the new targets are set. I would take a paid session on the scheduling tool if our contractor offered one, and in the first year I'd keep working site days while checking openings at the builders across town if my rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can adjust to a proven system, but I don't want to learn the rules only after my pay packet is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written record of the hours allowed for each frame and a chance for the lead to correct a wrong estimate. If a software schedule ignores a bowed wall, everyone on the crew loses time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for paid instruction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learned enough from guessing to know the cost of a bad guess. The company bought the tool and uses it to judge us, so it should pay for the hour to show us how it works.

say: I would demand a **crew check** before software plans become performance targets.
I would ask for **paid instruction** when new paperwork reaches the site.
think: I could lose **site days** while physical work remains human.
A simultaneous dip in Dev’s hours could exhaust **four months** of savings.
do: Ask a **union organiser** to gather crews on target setting.
Check **other builders** if the site rota shrinks.
feel: **Anxious** about pay falling before rules are explained.
S1.quote: I can adjust to a proven system, but I don't want to learn the rules only after my pay packet is smaller.
fieldNote: He accepts technology once **tested**, while insisting that the employer explain rules used to judge worker output.
His **junior status** makes fewer site days plausible, and Dev’s variable hours limit what four months saved can absorb.

steps.text: Ask union organiser to gather crews about software targets
Attend paid scheduling-tool instruction if contractor offers it
Check builder vacancies across town if site rota shrinks
Keep working paid site days while checking new targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI may write the plans in 2028, but robots arrive to do the fitting about 2031. We should bargain for paid learning now, while the contractor still needs us on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good enough to claim the last carpentry place if robots do the work as well as people. Planning might change my tasks in 2028, but by 2031 I expect my site income to drop badly; four months saved cannot cover years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask the union about paid placements in building repairs and apply for one if a contractor actually offers wages. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid framing work and check AGI drawings with a lead; if hours fell, Dev and I would ring the mortgage provider before the payment was late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. At 43 with children still in school, a three-year warning before robots is shorter than the time it took us to save four months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would repairs survive the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know. I have seen old roofs where access takes more thought than the repair, but capable robots might learn those jobs too. I want a placement that pays now, not a promise of a safe trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dev say about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev wants us to keep it for the mortgage and food, not spend it on a private course with no job attached. I agree, even though I would take a paid training risk.

say: I would explain that **2028 AGI** changes plans before **2031 robots** reach fitting.
I would ask for **paid learning** while contractors still need crews.
think: I expect a serious **site wage loss** when capable robots arrive.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot fund years of mortgage payments.
do: Apply for a **paid repair placement** if a contractor offers one.
Keep **framing shifts** and check AGI drawings with a lead in 2029.
Call the **mortgage provider** as soon as hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost wages and a short financial runway.
S2.quote: I'm not good enough to claim the last carpentry place if robots do the work as well as people.
fieldNote: Zane states plainly that his **developing carpentry skill** will not protect a junior place against capable robots.
He wants **paid placement** and lender contact, preserving the reserve for food and mortgage rather than buying an uncertain course.

steps.text: Apply for paid building-repair placement if a contractor offers wages
Keep taking paid framing shifts in 2029
Check AGI drawings with lead during 2029 site work
Call mortgage provider with Dev when hours first fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we can use five years to win a real training agreement, with wages attached. AGI handles more plans in 2031 and the robots come for the fitting around 2034; those are separate fights over work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might still carry and fit while AGI changes office work, though cheaper plans could mean thinner crews. By 51 the robots may do the site work I have finally learned; I expect my hours to fall, but five years could let me qualify for a paid maintenance role first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our union branch this year to propose a paid rotation through snag repairs, meaning fixing faults found before handover. If it is agreed, I'd take one day a week and keep a log of completed fixes; in 2032 I'd apply for housing maintenance posts, then use AGI work orders with supervision in the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a sequence of steps. A paid rotation would let me prove I can repair a door without asking the mortgage to fund my lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the branch cannot win a rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the housing contractor directly whether they hire trainees on wages. I will not resign from the framing crew for an unpaid place; the children still need shoes and meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old are the children in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be fifteen and twenty. Our older child might be working or studying, so costs would change, but I wouldn't count on money coming home from them.

say: I would press for a **paid training agreement** before robot fitting arrives.
I would distinguish **2031 plans** from **2034 fitting**.
think: My **site hours** may thin when AGI makes planning cheaper.
A **maintenance role** might provide wages before 2034 robots reduce fitting jobs.
do: Seek a **paid snag-repair rotation** through the union branch.
Use **AGI work orders** under supervision after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to prove repair skills while paid.
S3.quote: A paid rotation would let me prove I can repair a door without asking the mortgage to fund my lessons.
fieldNote: His plan uses **union bargaining** to create a paid route into repair work, rather than assuming training is freely available.
He expects **robot competition** at 51 and correctly sees children’s expenses changing as they reach fifteen and twenty.

steps.text: Ask union branch to seek a paid snag-repair rotation
Take one paid weekly snag-repair day if rotation is agreed
Apply for housing maintenance posts in 2032
Use AGI work orders under supervision after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for an apprenticeship of sorts, even for a man who started late. I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 at the 2039 robot date, and I still expect to need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be seventeen and twenty-two by 2036, so the household won't have exactly today's school expenses. The mortgage may be lower if we keep paying, but there is no pension I can count on here; robots that fit and carry could still take my site hours when I'm 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the framing job now and add a small amount to our reserve each month when Dev's office hours allow it. Over the next three years I'd take paid repair shifts if offered; in 2037 I'd check actual maintenance vacancies and learn their work-order system before deciding whether to leave the building crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than alarmed today. I have time to build a record, but I cannot make a lost wage in my fifties harmless by calling it a long-term problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. At seventeen and twenty-two they may need help getting started themselves. I'd rather ask the lender for a different payment schedule if our wages fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer with paid hours and a supervisor who knows I'm still learning repairs. I won't trade a real site wage for an advertisement that just says people should be flexible.

say: I would say the **decade** gives a late starter time to build skills.
I would remind coworkers that **56** is still an age when I need wages.
think: My children’s **school costs** change as they become older.
I cannot count on a **pension** to replace robot-threatened site pay.
do: Keep **framing wages** and add to the reserve when hours allow.
Check **maintenance vacancies** and their work-order system in 2037.
feel: **Uneasy** about wages in my fifties, with time to prepare.
S4.quote: I cannot make a lost wage in my fifties harmless by calling it a long-term problem.
fieldNote: He sees a longer path to **paid repair competence** while explicitly refusing to assume retirement income at 56.
His **children’s ages** and Dev’s varying hours shape how much he can save or risk over the decade.

steps.text: Keep paid framing shifts on current building crew
Add a small amount to reserve monthly when Dev has office hours
Take paid repair shifts over next three years if offered
Check and apply for suitable maintenance vacancies in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. If robots reach the tools by 2031, I may lose the wages that pay the mortgage before I have a proper repair record. A paid rotation, a clear account of which site hours remain, and early help from the lender would give us something real to work with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the AI measurements when a mistake can hurt someone. I'm slow, but I have learned to stop and ask the lead when a number looks wrong. Any new system should leave workers time to do that without being punished for falling behind.

headlineQuote: I'm slow, but I have learned to stop and ask the lead when a number looks wrong.
portrait: Zane is a **43-year-old junior** framer who entered construction late and still asks for help with drawings.
A **mortgage**, two children and variable household hours make his four-month reserve valuable but limited.
He tries **AI occasionally**, checking it against a lead’s work before trusting it.
He seeks **paid repair experience** through collective bargaining while continuing site wages.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove his site wage by 2031 before he builds a repair record.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid rotation**, clear site hours and early lender help would protect the household through a wage gap.
